name: Uniform reservoir sampling Algorithm R
definition: For t>k choose J uniformly from {1,…,t}; if J≤k replace slot J; P(R_t=S)=1/C(t,k) for every k-subset S of the first t observation identities
variables: t stream count; k reservoir capacity; J unbiased integer draw; R_t retained identity set; C(t,k) binomial coefficient
assumptions: Fixed positive integer capacity, finite stream independent of sampling draws, conditionally uniform independent integer draws, exact counters and distinct observation identities even when values repeat
limitations: O(N) sequential processing and O(k) stored records; samples are dependent without replacement, order of slots is not a random permutation guarantee, no stratification or temporal weighting
failure_conditions: Invalid capacity, biased integer draws or counter overflow
Request for exactly k records from a stream of length less than k
computation: Start empty and retain each of the first min(k,N) records. At each later arrival t, generate an unbiased integer J from 1 through t (avoid modulo or floating-point scaling bias). Replace slot J if J≤k, otherwise leave the reservoir unchanged. At end return the retained identities; if N<k report the actual count and insufficient population for a full-size sample. Record random generator and seed for reproducibility where applicable.

source.citation: Vitter (1985), Random Sampling with a Reservoir, ACM TOMS 11(1), 37–57, section 2, pp. 39–40; Algorithm R attributed there to Alan Waterman. DOI 10.1145/3147.3165. https://www.cs.umd.edu/~samir/498/vitter.pdf

application: General uniform sampling of a finite stream; no empirical benefit claimed.
incompatible_methods: Treating samples as independent draws with replacement
mechanism_note: For a subset S not containing t, the preceding subset must equal S and survive with probability (t−k)/t. If S contains t, there are t−k possible preceding subsets, each with a unique replacement of probability 1/t. Both cases yield 1/C(t,k) by induction from t=k. Distinct from simulation by repeated independent draws and from quantile summaries. Short streams retain every observed identity.

name: Boyer–Moore majority cancellation
definition: Start c=0; if c=0 set (m,c)=(x,1), else c←c+1 for x=m and c←c−1 otherwise; a strict majority satisfies count(m)>N/2
variables: m current candidate; c uncancelled count; N total observations; x current observation
assumptions: Finite replayable categorical stream or an externally guaranteed strict majority; stable equivalence relation for equality; exact integer counters
limitations: O(N) comparisons, O(1) candidate and counters; residual count is not frequency, mode is not necessarily a strict majority, a nonzero residual alone does not establish majority
failure_conditions: No replay or strict majority guarantee when residual count is positive but no greater than N/2
computation: Start with no candidate and c=0. Process each item by the recurrence. If c=0 at termination return no strict majority, including an empty stream. If c>N/2 the candidate is already certified; otherwise count its true occurrences on an unchanged replay and return it only if the count exceeds floor(N/2). If replay is unavailable and no strict majority is guaranteed, report an unverified candidate rather than a majority.

source.citation: Boyer and Moore (1991), MJRTY: A Fast Majority Vote Algorithm, in Automated Reasoning, pp. 105–117, sections 5.2–5.4 and Figure 5.1. https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~boyer/mjrty.pdf

application: General categorical stream majority detection; no empirical benefit claimed.
required_inputs: Equality-comparable stream and replay for verification.
incompatible_methods: Reporting an unverified candidate as a strict majority
mechanism_note: Each processed prefix partitions into c identical uncancelled observations and unequal pairs. Removing a pair cannot eliminate a strict majority, so a true majority must survive; c=0 rules one out. A nonmajority can survive (A,B,C leaves C), making verification essential unless the residual itself certifies it. Distinct from a full histogram or empirical distribution.
